A changed name expresses an argument about loss
Naomi asks the town to hear bitterness in her name. The account also names Ruth beside her return. Naomi's sense of emptiness stands beside a relationship she does not yet recognize as provision.
A harvest rule becomes a means of survival

Ruth’s access to leftover grain keeps two widows alive. Permission, safety, and extra food matter as much as the field itself. Boaz’s actions show how a rule depends on those with power. Ruth remains a worker with needs and choices. The harvest scenes make loyalty concrete through food and protection.
Ruth gives the plan her own words
Naomi prepares the visit, but Ruth states the request herself. She asks Boaz to accept a family duty rather than only give food. The night scene leads toward a public decision at the gate.

The gate scene places a family’s future before witnesses. Land, marriage, and the dead man’s name belong to one decision. Boaz accepts duties that the other relative declines. The story moves private loyalty into public responsibility. The final family line connects this small household with David.
